title: Why Simca becomes Talbot and how the marque disappears
author: codex-blog-rewrite
excerpt: The disappearance of the Simca name is not a sudden collapse. It is prepared through the long Chrysler sequence and then through the PSA takeover, when the marque’s identity becomes blurred.
content:
Simca does not vanish in a single moment. The end of the name is better understood as a chain of industrial and commercial shifts that gradually move the marque away from what once made it legible.

The Chrysler period changes the scale of the problem

As Chrysler takes a growing place inside Simca, the marque still keeps a strong French presence, yet the decision-making frame moves. Products, investments and image no longer answer quite the same method as in the Pigozzi years.

That shift does not erase Simca at once, but it already weakens the agreement among its details between marque, customers and industrial project.

Talbot as a takeover solution, not a natural continuity

The PSA takeover in 1978 brings back the Talbot name. The move looks more like a portfolio solution than a faithful continuation of Simca history. For the public, the change blurs the heritage rather than clarifying it.

A popular marque lives through continuity as much as through products. Once the name changes and identity disperses, the relationship with the public unravels quickly.

Why the Simca memory remains stronger than Talbot

In French automotive memory, Simca keeps a clearer face than Talbot because it points to an identifiable era: Aronde, Simca 1000, 1100 and popular cars widely seen on the roads.

Talbot, by contrast, feels more like an unfinished transition. That is also why the Simca name remains alive among enthusiasts even after it vanished from showrooms.
